analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $7.00 an hour in steps.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $7.00 an hour never got a vote: it was referred to a House committee and then a subcommittee, where it sat until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage — unchanged at $5.15 an hour since 1997 — in three steps: to $5.85 sixty days after passage, $6.45 a year later, and $7.00 two years later. It would also have ended the Northern Mariana Islands' exemption from the federal minimum wage, phasing island workers up from $3.55 to the federal floor in 50-cent steps every six months. The House Democratic sponsor had 95 cosponsors, but the bill was sent to committee, then to a subcommittee, and was never brought to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would see their hourly pay rise from $5.15 to as much as $7.00 over two years — a raise of about 36% at the top step. Workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, who had been legally exempt from the federal minimum wage, would gain the most, starting from a $3.55 floor. Households dependent on full-time minimum-wage work would see annual pay rise by roughly $3,800 at the final step before any side effects.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps — $5.85, then $6.45, then $7.00 over roughly two years — from the $5.15 rate in effect since 1997, lifting pay for workers at the bottom of the wage scale.

Applies the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, with a transition that starts island workers at $3.55 and raises the wage 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal level.
The first increase comes 60 days after enactment, so workers would see a pay raise within months rather than waiting years.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum or near-minimum wages — concentrated in food service, retail, and other labor-intensive services — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost could reach consumers through prices or show up as fewer hours or jobs at the very bottom of the wage scale. Employers in the Northern Mariana Islands, whose wage floor had been far below the federal one, would face the steepest adjustment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers, especially in the islands

drawbacks.text: The increase is a real cost for employers of minimum-wage labor, and small businesses and labor-intensive sectors like restaurants have long argued that mandated wage floors lead to reduced hiring, cut hours, or higher prices for the lowest-paid jobs.

The bill phases the raise in over two years, but does not index the minimum wage to inflation afterward, so the real value of $7.00 would erode again until Congress acts — the same pattern that left the wage stuck at $5.15 for seven years.

Even the phased transition for the Northern Mariana Islands would roughly double the island wage floor over time, a disruption to a small economy that had built its industries around wages far below the U.S. mainland level.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated on the workers least able to bargain for raises: a full-time minimum-wage worker would take home roughly $3,800 more per year once the top step arrived. The costs fall on the businesses that employ them, and economists genuinely disagree about how much of that shows up as lost jobs versus higher prices and thinner margins. The strongest honest objection is that the bill addressed the symptom (a wage floor frozen since 1997) without fixing the cause, since it contained no automatic adjustment for future inflation. On balance, this is a straightforward, well-understood policy that shifts income from low-wage employers' margins to low-wage workers' paychecks.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2004 on April 30, 2004, with 95 cosponsors (94 Democrats and 1 Independent).
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On May 14, 2004, it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last action of any kind on the bill.
No markup, no floor debate, and no vote ever occurred; the Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying the $5.15 minimum wage were better off, since the wage stayed frozen. The committee majority was also better off in the sense that it never had to take a recorded position, and workers in the Northern Mariana Islands' low-wage industries kept their exemption from the federal wage floor.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-7); bill sponsor, senior Democrat on Education and the Workforce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 74 original cosponsors from his party, including senior members like Reps. Gephardt, Rangel, Obey, and Frank.

for.name: 95 cosponsors (94 House Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill broad support among House Democrats but no recorded Republican support.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce majority
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the Fair Labor Standards Act
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote — so it never left committee.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, leaving it to die in the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party control of the House floor calendar in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Did not bring a stand-alone minimum wage increase to the floor during the 108th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 95 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The industry is the largest employer of minimum-wage workers, so a 36% rise in the wage floor directly raises its labor costs; the industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the pay of the very workers it employs.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These employers would absorb higher payroll costs for their lowest-paid staff; the savings from the wage staying at $5.15 came out of those workers' paychecks.

industries.industry: Garment and tourism industries in the Northern Mariana Islands
industries.note: The islands had been exempt from the federal minimum wage, letting local industries pay as little as $3.55 an hour; the bill would have phased that exemption out, ending a cost advantage built on wages below the U.S. floor.
